name: Harbor Loom Software
location: Modeled operation: a Boston, Massachusetts-based United States client-delivery team. Harbor Loom Software is a fictional analogue of thoughtbot's documented Boston software-design and development activity.
operations: thoughtbot provides software design, development, modernization and product-management services. Its published guidance connects prioritized work with implementation, review and acceptance. Harbor Loom Software is the fictional analogue; the modeled unit is one four-person delivery team within its United States consultancy. Synthetic scale: the team maintains and extends one established web application for managing business customer workflows, serving a United States software-company client with 120 customer organizations and approximately 3,500 active users. The engagement has operated for twelve months and includes a product delivery lead, product designer and two developers. Ordinary work includes interpreting customer feedback, refining requirements, implementing changes, reviewing code, assessing defects, maintaining documentation and preparing release recommendations. A typical week completes six to ten mixed stories, fixes and maintenance items while retaining approximately 80 open backlog items. The workspace contains earlier releases, superseded requirements, research findings, architectural decisions and unresolved maintenance work beyond any selected episode. The proposed cycles cover product and engineering decisions using existing records within this ongoing operation; production execution remains outside their completion boundary.

outlines.title: Resolve release scope against conflicting acceptance and technical evidence
outlines.objective: Produce a defensible release-readiness recommendation and a consistent remediation backlog for the existing client application.
outlines.decision_problem: A proposed release combines valuable changes with incompatible dependencies, uneven acceptance evidence and apparently successful checks that may refer to earlier code. The product lead creates the plan and weighs a smaller coherent release against deferral. The backend developer traces server-side dependencies and evidence applicability; the frontend developer checks browser behavior and client/server compatibility; the designer assesses whether the included changes complete usable journeys. Their findings must change which work is recommended, held or returned for correction. GitHub review comments preserve technical objections, while Jira descriptions, priorities and appropriate statuses reflect the resulting scope and feasible repair allocation. The completed cycle leaves a decision with evidence references, unresolved conditions and downstream remediation requirements. A hold addresses supported smaller-release alternatives and delayed value; partial repair allocations preserve incomplete and unfunded work. Planning repairs does not establish repaired readiness. The cycle does not merge, deploy or manufacture fresh test results.

outlines.title: Choose the next product increment from conflicting customer evidence
outlines.objective: Replace an assumption-heavy feature backlog with a justified, capacity-bounded increment and implementable acceptance criteria.
outlines.decision_problem: Existing interviews, usage exports and support examples point to different causes of customer difficulty. A prominent feature request may benefit a small segment while a less visible workflow problem affects more customers; duplicate observations, consent restrictions and incomplete evidence may also make either conclusion premature. The product lead creates the plan and evaluates value, capacity and prior commitments. The designer synthesizes research, distinguishes observations from hypotheses and defines complete user journeys. The backend developer assesses data availability, hidden dependencies and the cost of alternative slices. Their outputs jointly determine whether to advance a feature, narrow it, prioritize a workflow correction or pursue justified investigation. Updated Jira work and a reviewed rationale become the next implementation team's requirements. Any investigation choice preserves maintenance obligations, deferred requests and a usable evidence handoff. No new interviews or live analytics are required to finish.

outlines.title: Select a migration approach that preserves customer workflows
outlines.objective: Choose an implementable approach to an existing application programming interface or data-contract change and translate its consequences into engineering and acceptance work.
outlines.decision_problem: A proposed cleanup simplifies server maintenance but changes fields or behavior still used by current browser flows and historical records. Existing architecture notes, source snapshots and defect evidence allow comparison of immediate replacement, a compatibility layer and staged migration. The product lead creates the plan and balances maintenance savings against scope and continuity. The backend developer maps data invariants, conversion requirements and recovery limits. The frontend developer identifies consumers, mixed-version behavior and error-handling consequences. The designer determines how partial migration, unavailable data and recovery affect user understanding and task completion. Their findings must alter the chosen approach, prerequisite work and retirement conditions. The cycle finishes with a reviewed technical decision, linked Jira tasks and corrected GitHub review guidance that downstream implementers can use; migration execution and new tests remain subsequent work.

The selected cycles use existing design evidence and produce requirements and acceptance decisions. They do not require an interactive design-authoring application or imply that documents replace a production design tool.

Client constraints and any delegated acceptance rights are seeded as existing records. A cycle can finish with a justified hold or recommendation requiring later client action; completion cannot depend on a new external response or elapsed time.

Worker materials and episode instructions use plain wording or introduce abbreviations on first use. Describe selected files and open-document controls directly; write pull-request descriptions in full; introduce Hypertext Transfer Protocol before using HTTP when discussing response behavior.
